note_tweet.text:
A small but annoying lesson from building automated video narration: text-to-speech does not know how to read technical text. It will happily say "owner slash repo" out loud, or stumble through a file name or command, and it sounds broken every time.

The fix wasn't a smarter voice model, it was a writing rule. Narration should only ever contain things that read naturally as words. Repo paths, handles, file names, commands, code, links, none of that belongs in spoken narration. If it needs to be shown, the screen shows it. The voice just says the product name.

I also added a check that catches this automatically before a video ships, so narration with a repo path or handle gets flagged and sent back with what to say instead, rather than me catching it by ear after the fact.

One specific case worth sharing: https://t.co/iGrPUVv6la now gets spoken as "repo on GitHub," and if GitHub is already mentioned in the sentence, it just says "repo." Small detail, but it's the difference between narration that sounds natural and one that sounds like a bot reading a URL.

Building this in public at https://t.co/ePIbY8E6GG

Kotoba is the Japanese voice AI lab behind the Koto model.

The transaction is expected to close later in the fourth quarter of 2026 subject to regulatory approvals.

Koto supports Japanese text to speech speech to text and speech to speech conversion.

Kotoba was founded in July 2023 by Noriyuki Kojima and Jungo Kasai.

Kojima holds a computer science PhD from Cornell and co-built Fugaku-LLM.

Kasai holds a PhD from the University of Washington and was an assistant professor at the Toyota Technological Institute at the University of Chicago.

Artificial Analysis launched Time to First Audio, a benchmark for how quickly text-to-speech models start speaking.

> It measures the time from sending the full text to the first audible speech, so silence at the start counts as waiting. Every model is tested daily on the same 12 prompts across four input lengths, and the headline number is a 7-day average.

> Among leading models, the wait runs from 76 ms to nearly a second, by Artificial Analysis' measurements. Speechify's Simba 3.5 starts in 116 ms, the highest Arena Elo of any model under 200 ms, while ElevenLabs' Eleven v4 Turbo takes 258 ms against 653 ms for Eleven v4.

> Streaming is the dividing line. The 65 streaming models typically begin speaking within a few hundred milliseconds, at a median of 376 ms. The 20 non-streaming models must finish generating before they return anything, and their median is 2.0 seconds.
